request.lesson: A backlog entry's description of a PROBLEM ages well; its claim about why the problem is BLOCKED ages badly, because the blocker is inferred once and never re-checked. Re-derive it before building on it. Seen three times in one clearing session: an entry listed four CLIs as missing a warning when two already had it and one had no such flag; another said a helper needed lifting into a shared module when four of six call sites already had it and the two that did not were following a documented spec invariant; a third named a suite as blocked on missing step vocabulary when it was blocked on package provisioning. Each time the problem statement was still true, the blocker claim was wrong, and following it produced work that had to be reverted.

str.replace on indented Python matches ACROSS indent levels, because an 8-space pattern is a substring of the same text at 12 spaces. Rewriting call sites with str.replace('        return x()', '        return self._x()') also rewrites the helper's own body into a self-call — infinite recursion, and it happened once per client in a two-client change. The same class ate a newline in a YAML sweep and emitted '# v4.4.0with:', which would have broken every workflow. Anchor the rewrite to a whole line (iterate splitlines, re.match with ^) and check the diff SHAPE afterwards: a pure call-site swap must be N insertions for N deletions, so a net line-count change means the pattern consumed something it should not have.

Reading a command's exit code through a pipe reads the LAST command's code, not the one under test: `script.py | tail -2` then `echo $?` reports tail's success even when script.py exited non-zero. The work-loop skill already warns about this, and it still cost a wrong conclusion recorded into the backlog — a retired writer was reported as 'exits 0, so callers think it wrote' when it exits 2 and fails loudly. The whole finding was an artefact of the pipe. Run the command bare and read $? on the next line; if output must be trimmed, capture the code first (`rc=$?`) or use PIPESTATUS. Knowing the rule is not the same as following it under time pressure — the tell is any $? read on a line containing a pipe.

A batched subprocess changes the blast radius of one bad input, and the batch API may return a PARTIAL result on failure. `git check-ignore --stdin -z` exits 128 for the whole invocation on a single unusable path (outside the repo, inside a nested git root, or carrying pathspec magic) while still echoing the candidates it processed first. Discarding that output silently loses information; trusting it silently under-reports. Under a per-path loop the damage was one path. So when replacing N calls with one, decide explicitly what a non-success exit means and treat a partial answer as unusable rather than as data. The same reasoning applies to any fan-in rewrite, not just git.

Narrowing an except clause at a lock-holding boundary requires checking the exception taxonomy first, not just the ones you have seen. Narrowing _recover_engine_state_tmp to (FileNotFoundError, ValueError) to stop it deleting valid artifacts also stopped it catching RecursionError, which json.loads raises on a deeply nested document and which is not a ValueError. main() handled only two exception types, so a planted .engine-state-*.json.tmp tracebacked out of sl.exclusive() — and because the dotfile was never removed, every later transition on that spec failed identically. The durable shape is: catch BROADLY so nothing escapes the lock holder, and act NARROWLY on a typed predicate. Two properties, two mechanisms; conflating them produced a bug in each direction on the same line.

Control-character neutralisation for an agent-captured stream belongs at every tool's output chokepoint, not only at a shared result type. Escaping was added to GuardResult's reason/message, which covered the guard layer — but loop-engine.py formats its own warnings and had zero uses of the sanitiser, so a planted .engine-state-<ESC>[2J<ESC>[31mFAKE-OK.json.tmp put a real screen-clear and colour change into the transcript. The filename came from a glob(), under the same planted-file threat model that function already accepted for the file's CONTENT. Two lessons: collapsing whitespace is not sanitising (str.split consumes only the whitespace controls, leaving ESC); and the sanitiser is worth duplicating per tool rather than importing, because these lines fire on paths where the shared module is unloadable, which is when a diagnostic matters most.

A reviewer subagent reports against the file as it stood when the review was dispatched, not as it stands when the report arrives. During RFC-0092's review, a round-3 finding named an inconsistency between two statements of the same control that an edit landing minutes after dispatch had already removed by giving the control a single home. Applying the reviewer's prescribed fix verbatim would have re-edited text that was already correct, and would have counted a resolved item as an open defect in the handoff. Re-checking each finding against current file state before remediating separates a live defect from a stale snapshot, and costs one grep when the finding cites a path and line.

friction.summary: A supplied-path-only adjudicator returned indeterminate for a repository fact the controller later resolved with one bounded read.

request.lesson: Adjudication path envelopes include every repository-confined current file cited by a source finding when that file is needed to test a predicate. A fact that the controller can settle with one bounded read should be settled inside adjudication; otherwise supplied-path restrictions create avoidable indeterminate stops and split the evidence decision across two actors.

A pack version bump is never one file, and the file set depends on the pack's distribution route. Every pack bumps packs/<pack>/pack.toml and packs/<pack>/.claude-plugin/plugin.json together, and every bump also needs a docs/product/changelog.md entry in the same PR (docs/CONVENTIONS.md, RFC-0095). A pack listed in the root .claude-plugin/marketplace.json bumps that too, making four files. A repo-scope pack is NOT listed there -- the Claude plugin marketplace is the user-profile install route -- so its bump is three files and there is no marketplace entry to update. Eight of twenty-two packs ship a plugin.json with no marketplace entry: core, example-pack, catalogue-curation, governance-extras, iac-terraform, monorepo-extras, release-engineering, and user-guide-diataxis. Looking for a marketplace entry for one of those wastes the search. Enforcement is uneven, which is why the file set has to be known rather than discovered: CAT-V-005 catches a pack.toml/plugin.json mismatch so make build-check fails, marketplace.json staleness is caught only by the agentbundle pytest suite, and the changelog obligation is a convention gate. FORCE=1 make build-self projects pack CONTENT into .claude/ and .agents/ but propagates no version, so it repairs none of these. Determine the pack's route first, then bump its set by hand in one commit.

friction.summary: schedule failed after approve-plan had already pinned the plan hash.

request.lesson: loop-cohort schedule parses task headings by a fixed pattern, not by prose: it looks for '## T<n>' or '### T<n>' and stops with 'no tasks found' on anything else. A plan whose tasks read '### Task 1 - Title' passes every human review and every lint, then fails at schedule time - after approve-plan has already pinned the plan hash, so the fix requires the documented cohort recovery (reset, init, approve-plan, schedule) rather than a simple edit. Write task headings as '### T<n>: Title' from the first draft, and check the heading pattern against the shipped precedent in an existing plan before the G-plan sequence rather than after it. The general rule: when a tool consumes a document, the document's structure is an interface with a parser on the other side, so confirm the parser's shape before an irreversible pinning step consumes it.

friction.summary: The dominated-bound shape recurred in five consecutive rounds, twice introduced by the fix for the previous instance.

request.lesson: A numeric bound is underspecified until you state what it is measured from, and the origin is usually the more serious defect. A path-depth bound of 10 measured from the enumeration root was layout-dependent: admitting an optional category directory consumed one level, so an identical payload measured deeper purely because its publisher grouped by topic, and the same source changed verdict on being reorganised. Measured from the leaf envelope instead, the bound means how deep a unit's own payload may nest and is invariant under choices the publisher is free to make. Fixing the origin mattered more than the number. Separately, five consecutive rounds produced dominated bounds, where two limits on one quantity left the dominated one unreachable and its diagnostic unsatisfiable. Before writing any limit, enumerate every other limit on the same quantity and compute which fires first for the boundary input, then state the enforcement mechanism that makes that ordering true. Never request a bound without specifying its value: twice a worker fabricated one, and a fabricated bound is worse than none because it looks like a decision.
